ai.literal: To the beloved who loved me, his withholding of love I consented to; my nature that has turned pale, to whom shall I tell, O friend?
ai.translation: I consented to my beloved withholding his love and departing; now, to whom can I complain about this sallow paleness that has overcome my nature?
ai.modern: என்னை விரும்பிய காதலர் எனக்கு அன்பு செய்யாமல் பிரிந்திருப்பதை நான் ஏற்றுக்கொண்டேன்; ஆனால் அதனால் பசலை நிறம் அடைந்துவிட்ட என் உடலின் நிலையை வேறு யாருக்குச் சொல்வேன்?
ai.explanation: The heroine laments her physical state of paleness (pasappu) caused by separation. She admits that she willingly consented (nērntēn) to her lover's departure or his withholding of immediate grace, understanding his situation. However, her body has reacted to the separation by turning pale, changing her natural complexion (paṇpu). She helplessly asks her friend to whom she can complain about this physical suffering, since she herself agreed to the very separation that caused it.

ai.literal: With the proud right saying 'He gave (it)', this pallor, having presented itself, spreads upon my body.
ai.translation: With the proud claim that 'He gave me to her,' this pallor has presented itself and spreads all over my body.
ai.modern: அவர் (என் காதலர்) தான் என்னைத் தந்தார் என்ற உரிமையோடு, இந்தப் பசப்பு என் உடம்பின் மேல் வந்து பரவுகிறது.
ai.explanation: The heroine is suffering from the pain of separation, which manifests as a sickly yellow-green pallor on her skin. She personifies this pallor as an uninvited guest who behaves with absolute authority. The pallor spreads boldly across her body, acting as if it has a legitimate right to be there because it was given to her as a parting gift by her lover himself. By using the words 'avar' (he) and 'ivar' (this person), she highlights the intimate connection between her lover's departure and the arrival of her physical grief.

ai.literal: And beauty and modesty he took away, as a return, affliction and pallor having given.
ai.translation: My beloved took away my beauty and my modesty, giving me in return only affliction and pallor.
ai.modern: அவர் என் அழகையும் நாணத்தையும் எடுத்துக் கொண்டார்; அதற்குப் பதிலாகத் துன்பத்தையும் பசலை நிறத்தையும் தந்துவிட்டுச் சென்றார்.
ai.explanation: In this verse, the heroine laments her state of separation. She expresses that her beloved, upon leaving, took with him her natural grace and her modesty. In exchange for these precious qualities, he left her with the painful affliction of longing and the sickly yellow pallor that stains her skin. The word 'kaimmāṟā' is used with bitter irony, highlighting the unfair trade of her virtues for suffering.

ai.literal: I think of him indeed, what I speak of is his qualities indeed; is this pallor deceitful, or is there some other reason?
ai.translation: I think of him constantly, and I speak only of his noble qualities. Yet, this pallor has spread over me; is it acting deceitfully, or is there some other secret cause?
ai.modern: நான் அவரை எப்போதும் நினைக்கிறேன்; நான் பேசுவதும் அவருடைய பெருமைகளைப் பற்றித்தான். அப்படியிருக்க, என் உடலில் பசப்பு படர்வது வஞ்சகமா அல்லது வேறு ஏதேனும் காரணம் உண்டா?
ai.explanation: The heroine is suffering from the pain of separation, and her skin has turned pale, a physical sign of longing known as 'pasappu'. She argues that this pallor is unjustified because she has not forgotten her lover for even a moment; she constantly thinks of him and speaks only of his virtues. Since her mind and speech are entirely filled with him, she wonders if the pallor is playing a deceitful trick on her by appearing anyway. Alternatively, she questions if there is some other hidden reason for this discoloration that she does not understand.

ai.literal: Look there, my lover departs; look here, my body, pallor spreading.
ai.translation: Look there! My lover is departing. Look here! Pallor is already spreading over my body.
ai.modern: அதோ பாருங்கள், என் காதலர் போகிறார்; இதோ பாருங்கள், என் உடம்பில் பசலை நிறம் பரவுகிறது.
ai.explanation: This couplet vividly captures the immediate physical toll of separation on the heroine. By using the contrasting deictic words 'uvakkāṇ' (look there) and 'ivakkāṇ' (look here), she points out the simultaneous nature of her lover's departure and her own distress. The moment he takes a step away, the sickly yellow pallor (pasappu) associated with grief and longing instantly begins to crawl over her skin. This dramatic exaggeration highlights the depth of her attachment and how her physical well-being is entirely bound to his presence.

ai.literal: Like darkness indeed that watches for the extinction of the lamp, the pallor watches for the end of the husband's embrace.
ai.translation: Just like darkness that waits for the lamp to go out, this pallor waits for the moment my husband's embrace ends to spread over me.
ai.modern: விளக்கு அணையும் தருணத்தை எதிர்பார்த்துக் காத்திருக்கும் இருளைப் போல, தலைவனுடைய அணைப்பு முடியும் தருணத்தை எதிர்பார்த்துக் காத்திருக்கிறது இந்தப் பசலை நிறம்.
ai.explanation: This couplet beautifully illustrates the instantaneous nature of the heroine's grief during separation. She compares the pallor (pasappu) that spreads over her skin to darkness (iruḷ) waiting to engulf a room. Just as darkness watches for the lamp (viḷakku) to be extinguished to immediately take over, the pallor watches for the exact moment her husband's (koṇkaṇ) embrace (muyakku) ends (aṟṟam) to cover her. The comparison highlights how the joy of union is like light, and the pain of separation is like an ever-waiting darkness.

ai.literal: Having embraced I lay; I moved aside; at that very moment, to scoop and take, indeed like, spread the pallor.
ai.translation: I lay in his embrace, but the moment I turned aside, the pallor of separation spread over me so thickly that it could be scooped up by the handful.
ai.modern: நான் என் காதலரைத் தழுவிக்கொண்டு படுத்திருந்தேன்; அவரிடமிருந்து சற்றே விலகினேன்; அந்த நொடியிலேயே, அள்ளி எடுக்கும் அளவுக்குப் பசலை நிறம் என் மேல் படர்ந்துவிட்டது.
ai.explanation: This couplet vividly describes the heroine's intense sensitivity to even the briefest separation from her lover. She explains that she was lying in a close embrace, but the very instant she turned or moved slightly aside, the pallor of separation (pacappu) rushed to cover her body. The poet uses a striking hyperbole, stating that the sallow spots spread so thickly in that split second that they could be scooped up by the handful (aḷḷikkoḷ). This highlights how her physical and emotional well-being is entirely dependent on constant union with her beloved.

ai.explanation: In this couplet, the heroine laments the unfairness of public gossip. People around her easily notice her physical change and remark that she has turned pale with grief. However, they fail to point out or blame the lover who departed and caused her this pain. The verse highlights her loneliness, as the world judges her visible suffering without holding the responsible partner accountable.

ai.literal: Let turn pale indeed completely my body, he who made me love, of good state will become, if.
ai.translation: Let my body turn completely pale, if only he who made me love him can remain in good health and happiness.
ai.modern: என்னை விரும்பச் செய்த என் காதலர் நல்ல நிலையில் நலமாக இருப்பார் என்றால், என் உடம்பு முழுவதும் பசலை நிறம் அடைந்து போகட்டும்.
ai.explanation: In this couplet, the heroine expresses her selfless love amidst the pain of separation. She is suffering from 'pasappu' (the sallow, pale discoloration of the skin caused by grief), which is spreading over her body. However, she declares that she does not care if her body ('mēni') turns completely pale ('pasakka'), as long as her lover ('nayappittār', the one who made her desire him) is safe and in a good state ('nannilaiyar') wherever he is. Her own physical suffering is secondary to his well-being.

ai.literal: Obtaining the name as 'pallor' is indeed good, if [people] do not slander the lack of grace of him who made me love.
ai.translation: It is indeed good for me to acquire the reputation of being pale with grief, if only townspeople do not gossip about the unkindness of the one who won my love.
ai.modern: என்னை விரும்பச் செய்தவருடைய அன்பில்லாத் தன்மையை ஊரார் பழித்துப் பேச மாட்டார்கள் என்றால், எனக்குப் 'பசலை நோய் கொண்டவள்' என்னும் பெயர் கிடைப்பது நல்லதே ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: The heroine is suffering from 'pasappu', the sallow, pale complexion that appears on a woman's skin due to the grief of separation. She states that she does not mind being known as pale or lovesick, and is willing to bear that reputation. Her only concern is that the townspeople might blame her lover ('nayappittār') for being cruel and abandoning her. If they refrain from slandering his lack of grace ('nalkāmai'), she is perfectly happy to bear the physical mark of her longing.
